findings.claim: In most UK business electricity contracts, 'fixed' fixes the commodity part (wholesale energy plus supplier margin). Whether non-commodity charges (network, balancing, policy levies) are also fixed depends on the contract terms.
findings.evidence: Tritility (25 May 2026): 'the word ‘fixed’ in most business energy contracts refers specifically to the commodity element of your bill, the wholesale cost of the electricity itself, plus your supplier’s margin', typically around 40% of the total bill. 'Whether the remaining non-commodity charges are also fixed, which include network costs and government levies, depends on your contract terms.' In a fully fixed ('all-in') contract the supplier builds an estimate of non-commodity charges into the unit rate and standing charge. If network charges rise, the supplier absorbs it, and the price is usually set higher to include a buffer. EnergyCosts.co.uk (updated 5 October 2026) says similar: a contract can be called 'fixed' but still allow some regulated charges to move, so check whether a quoted rate is fully fixed or excludes some third-party charges. The Ofgem blog (31 March 2026) confirms that the bill covers wholesale, network and environmental costs, with wholesale typically about 40% of an electricity bill.
findings.limitations: The Tritility and EnergyCosts pages are commercial broker and comparison sites, not regulators or network operators. They are useful but not authoritative. No Ofgem, NESO or DNO page explaining contract treatment was found. The Ofgem blog only gives the broad cost split.

findings.claim: Contract structures: fully fixed, fixed with pass-through terms (part-fixed), fully pass-through, and flexible. 'Pass-through plus' was not defined in the sources read.
findings.evidence: Tritility: a pass-through contract (also called third-party charge or non-commodity pass-through) separates non-commodity costs from the wholesale price. The commodity rate stays fixed but 'network and policy charges move in line with the rates set by NESO, your DNO, and the government', so the business takes on the risk of changes. If charges fall you pay less, and if they rise the bill reflects it directly. In a fixed contract with pass-through terms, the commodity rate is fixed but the supplier may pass through changes to regulated charges such as TNUoS and DUoS mid-contract. EnergyCosts.co.uk gives four structures: fully fixed (forecast non-commodity costs included in the agreed price, risk of higher price); part-fixed, part-pass-through (some charges fixed, others move, risk of unexpected increases); fully pass-through (billed at actual cost, more transparent but less certainty); and flexible (wholesale traded separately, needs active management). Smaller businesses usually see charges bundled into the unit rate and standing charge, whereas larger or half-hourly customers may see charges itemised. Ofgem's contract page describes flexible (structured) contracts for large businesses.
findings.limitations: Terminology varies between suppliers and brokers. 'Pass-through plus' (pass-through with an added supplier uplift or fee) is not defined in any page read, so that term is unanswered. Definitions come from commercial sources.

findings.claim: Which elements are typically exposed: TNUoS, DUoS, BSUoS and policy levies can be passed through. Tritility reports TNUoS rose around 62% from April 2026, and some fixed contracts re-priced mid-contract.
findings.evidence: Tritility: charges such as TNUoS and DUoS 'can all move mid-contract if the relevant regulatory rates change'. 'From April 2026, TNUoS charges increased by an average of around 62% across Great Britain, following the start of the RIIO-ET3 regulatory period.' Customers on fully fixed contracts likely saw no immediate effect because the supplier absorbed it, whereas those with network-charge pass-through clauses saw it applied mid-contract. To check, look in the contract for sections on third-party charges, non-commodity costs or pass-through terms, with language letting the supplier change TNUoS, DUoS, BSUoS or policy levies. EnergyCosts.co.uk lists TNUoS (transmission), DUoS (distribution), BSUoS (balancing), Capacity Market, RO, FiT, CfD and CCL as the main non-commodity charges. CCL rates are published by HMRC on GOV.UK. The EnergyCosts page says Cornwall Insight forecast that by 2026 non-commodity charges would be nearly 60% of a typical business electricity bill.
findings.limitations: The 62% figure and the April 2026 price movement are reported by a broker (Tritility) and haven't been checked against NESO or Ofgem. It isn't established from official sources which charges any specific supplier fixes. CCL is a tax set by HMRC and usually appears as a pass-through or built-in item.

findings.claim: Clauses to look for and questions to ask: pass-through terms, reconciliation, change-in-law or regulatory re-opener clauses, force majeure, and which levies are in the fixed rate.
findings.evidence: Tritility: 'some business energy contracts contain clauses allowing suppliers to reopen pricing in response to significant regulatory changes, meaning even all-in customers should check their specific terms'. It adds that all suppliers reserve the right to raise costs or amend terms in exceptional circumstances outside their control (force majeure). Questions to ask: is TNUoS fixed or pass-through, what tariff assumption is in the quote, what happens if NESO revises TNUoS mid-term, is BSUoS fixed or passed through, and are policy levies (CCL, Capacity Market, CfD, Nuclear RAB) in the fixed rate. EnergyCosts.co.uk says to check for 'pass-through' and 'reconciliation' (supplier may adjust charges later), ask whether charges are reconciled later, which are passed through, and ask for a cost breakdown from the supplier or broker if charges aren't shown.
findings.limitations: Advice comes from commercial intermediaries and illustrates general practice. The exact wording of 'change in law' clauses varies by supplier and was not seen in a regulator document.

findings.claim: The MPAN (Meter Point Administration Number) identifies an electricity supply point. It is found on the electricity bill (sometimes called the 'supply number'), not on the physical meter. If there are no bills, it can be obtained from the supplier or online account, and also from the landlord, property manager or electricity distributor.
findings.evidence: Citizens Advice meter check page: 'Your Meter Point Administration Number (MPAN) will be on your electricity bill, where it’s sometimes called your ‘supply number’. It has 12 or 13 digits', and only the numbers on the bottom row are needed. 'If you don’t get bills, you can find out your MPAN by calling your supplier or checking your online account.' British Gas Business: an MPAN is usually a 21-digit number beginning with 'S', displayed in a grid. It appears on the business electricity bill under 'Details of charges' and 'You won’t be able to find your MPAN on your physical meter.' The supplier normally needs the last 13 digits. If you can't find it, speak to your property manager or landlord, or your electricity distributor. The page notes MPAN top line changes under Market-wide Half-Hourly Settlement (MHHS). It also lists the meter serial number, which is on the bill and on the meter near the barcode.
findings.limitations: Digit counts differ between sources (12 or 13 digits for the core on Citizens Advice, 21 digits including the top line on British Gas). Neither page is dated. British Gas is a supplier page, not a regulator. The Citizens Advice page is for domestic smart meter checking, so applying it to business supplies is an inference.

findings.claim: Consumption and contract details should be checked before quotes. Annual usage, standing charges, unit costs and the contract end date come from the current bill and contract, and quotes require business activity and energy usage.
findings.evidence: Citizens Advice: before switching, check the terms of the current contract including the end date, your standing charges and energy costs per unit as shown on the bill (in kWh), and your annual energy usage. For quotes you need to give information about what the business does and how much energy it uses. Ofgem's contract page: the type of contract available usually depends on the size of the business and how much energy it uses. Microbusiness status can depend on annual electricity use of up to 100,000 kWh, and small business status on up to 200,000 kWh. Some suppliers use either business size or annual consumption to decide which protections apply. The UIA guidance advises regular meter readings where readings are manual. The Ofgem blog (31 March 2026) says to submit regular meter readings or get a smart meter to be billed accurately.
findings.limitations: The pages say consumption determines business size, protections and the contract offered, but don't explain in detail how consumption or meter type changes quoted prices.

findings.claim: Smart and advanced meters matter for contract terms. Some fixed-term contracts require a smart or advanced meter, and these can be much cheaper than deemed or out-of-contract rates. Larger sites in profile classes 5-8 are in a separate category.
findings.evidence: DESNZ consultation (last updated 1 September 2026): smart-contingent contracts are fixed-term contracts requiring a smart or advanced meter, and the government says they are typically around 40% cheaper than deemed and out-of-contract rates. Suppliers must currently supply the largest sites (electricity meters in profile classes 5-8, or gas above 732 MWh a year) via advanced meters, subject to all reasonable steps. Since 1 October 2024 suppliers must give smaller organisations with smart meters free regular energy use information, and organisations of all sizes can request their smart meter data free (since 1 December 2022). Smart meter data supports Market-wide Half-Hourly Settlement.
findings.limitations: A consultation, not final rules. The Ofgem half-hourly guidance page opened with collapsed content, so no definition of half-hourly versus non-half-hourly metering or profile class from an official source was captured. The 'profile class' explanation and how meter type affects pricing aren't covered by an official source here.

findings.claim: Small businesses can use the Energy Ombudsman for disputes with energy brokers/TPIs from 19 December 2024, but only if the broker is a member of the Energy Ombudsman's scheme. Eligibility follows the small business definition.
findings.evidence: Energy Ombudsman broker page (published 7 November 2022; last updated 2 April 2026): 'If you’re a small business owner operating in the UK, from 19th December 2024 you’re eligible to receive free dispute resolution support for disputes with your energy broker or Third party intermediaries (TPIs).' Eligible businesses have fewer than 50 employees or their full-time equivalent AND an annual turnover of at most £6.5 million or a balance sheet total of £5.0 million, OR annual electricity consumption of not more than 200,000 kWh, OR annual gas consumption of not more than 500,000 kWh. Brokers choose which dispute resolution scheme to join, so you must check the Ombudsman's Energy Brokers Register: if the broker is a member the Ombudsman can help. The Ombudsman can't deal with commercial decisions about whether to provide a product or service, or with services for non-gas or electricity energy sources such as LPG.
findings.limitations: The page is dated (updated 2 April 2026) and the thresholds may change. It says brokers choose a scheme, so some brokers may use another scheme such as the UIA, which this page doesn't cover. It lists a 'small business' definition that is wider than the microbusiness definition.

findings.claim: Process and time limits for a broker complaint: complain to the broker first, then escalate after deadlock or 8 weeks. Evidence is due within 14 days and the broker has 28 days to implement an accepted decision.
findings.evidence: Energy Ombudsman broker page: step 1, raise the issue with your broker and allow time to resolve it. Step 2, register the dispute by website, telephone, email or post. Step 3, review any early resolution offers (Facilitated Complaint Resolution). Step 4, if no offers are accepted, both parties provide evidence within 14 days. Step 5, the Ombudsman reviews and notifies both parties of a decision. Step 6, if you accept the decision the broker has 28 days to implement the remedy. 'Only once both parties have reached deadlock, or the complaint has remained unresolved for eight weeks or longer may we look into your dispute.' The page says you need to follow the broker's complaints process first, and that 8 weeks or a deadlock letter applies.
findings.limitations: The page doesn't give a time limit for bringing a complaint after the event, such as a maximum period since the sale. The Terms of Reference extract does not show one either.

findings.claim: Award limit for broker complaints is up to £10,000, whereas small business complaints against suppliers can receive up to £20,000. The Ombudsman can't fine or punish brokers or suppliers.
findings.evidence: Energy Ombudsman broker page: outcomes include practical action, an apology, 'a payment of up to £10,000', and recommendations to prevent similar complaints. The Ombudsman can't punish brokers or suppliers, dictate how brokers operate, or issue fines. The Terms of Reference for Energy Brokers (last updated 29 January 2025): the Award 'shall be limited to £10,000 (inclusive of VAT, if any) per complaint for Domestic customers and any complaints regarding Energy Brokers' and to £20,000 for Small Business Consumers with a complaint against Energy Suppliers. Where a contract was mis-sold, the broker may be instructed to cover financial loss up to £10,000 and service shortfalls. The supplier-dispute page (S7) states financial awards up to £20,000 for suppliers and says the maximum award for brokers differs.
findings.limitations: The £10,000 limit is a cap on awards and doesn't mean that amount is typical. The Terms of Reference extract is dated 29 January 2025, so check for later changes.

findings.claim: Remit of broker complaints is narrower than supplier complaints: it covers sale and account management services of participating brokers, not the supplier's service after the sale.
findings.evidence: Terms of Reference for Energy Brokers: covered services are 'the services associated with the sale of and processing of gas and electricity contracts by a Participating Company, including where a contract has been mis-sold' and 'account management of the customer’s energy supply'. Complaints must come from a customer with a grievance about a sale attempted or carried out, or about account management services, or from someone acting for them with consent. The scheme 'shall not accept a complaint about a matter which concerns or relates to issues of service provided by an Energy Supplier following a sale by a Participating Company'. Complaints are accepted only against brokers that are participating companies that sold or tried to sell a contract on behalf of a licensed supplier, or have a contract to provide advice or account management. Brokers can be expelled for not paying fees, refusing to implement remedies, poor complaint handling or abuse of staff. Per the supplier page (S7), supplier disputes typically cover billing, sales process, customer service, switching and charges, with the same 8 week or deadlock route.
findings.limitations: Terms of Reference text is long and only the broker annex was seen. An Ofgem rule requires suppliers to work only with TPIs in a redress scheme (see Ofgem press release, 5 April 2024), but that is covered elsewhere.

notes:
T6: The only sources found that explain fixed versus pass-through treatment are commercial (Tritility, 25 May 2026; EnergyCosts.co.uk, updated 5 October 2026). Ofgem, NESO and DNO pages on the topic weren't found within the limits. 'Pass-through plus' isn't defined in any source read. Per-charge typical treatment (for example whether RO, FiT, CfD and capacity market are typically fixed in SME contracts) is only covered in general terms.
T7: Covered: where to find the MPAN, meter serial number and consumption data; why consumption matters for business size, protections and quotes; smart and advanced meter contract effects. Not covered: an official definition of half-hourly versus non-half-hourly metering and profile classes (Ofgem's page rendered with collapsed text), how to read profile class from the MPAN top line, and the effect of meter type on network charges and quotes. Those gaps remain after the page limits were reached.
T8: Answered from the Energy Ombudsman's own broker page (updated 2 April 2026) and the Energy Brokers Terms of Reference (updated 29 January 2025). Neither page states a time limit for bringing a complaint after the event. Brokers that belong to the UIA's scheme rather than the Energy Ombudsman's are outside these pages.
